result: OFF-UBCs (n=25) are hyperpolarized by mossy fiber input at 26 Hz (−9.5 ± 4.2 mV at steady-state), with some cells showing transient firing before hyperpolarization. OFF-UBCs fire within a narrower range of phases (274 ± 28°) compared to ON-UBCs and have significantly higher phase lag (p<0.001), though firing modulation amplitudes are similar between the two populations.
evaluation: Claims C20-C23, C32-C33 provide converging experimental evidence from current-clamp recordings showing OFF-UBC hyperpolarization, spontaneous firing patterns, and phase response characteristics. The data include appropriate sample sizes (n=25), statistical comparisons (p<0.001), and are supported by Figure 1 showing representative traces and population analyses.

result: OFF-UBCs display mGluR2-mediated outward currents that are blocked by LY341495, with 48% also showing NBQX-sensitive AMPAR currents. The mGluR2 current amplitude increases with stimulation frequency (41.5 ± 26.9 pA at 10 Hz to 129.9 ± 43.4 pA at 100 Hz, p<0.001), and the decay time constant correlates with OFF-UBC phase shift (r=0.621, p<0.05).
evaluation: Claims C39-C43 are supported by voltage-clamp pharmacological experiments with appropriate receptor antagonists (LY341495, NBQX) and statistical analyses. The correlations between mGluR2 kinetics and phase shifts are significant and mechanistically link receptor properties to functional output, as shown in Figure 2.

result: OFF-UBC responses show frequency-dependent modulation, with amplitude increasing from 0.3 Hz to 1 Hz then dropping at 3 Hz (p=0.0003). At higher frequencies, more cells are silenced (20% at 1 Hz, 68% at 3 Hz), and phase shifts increase significantly with frequency (193 ± 46° at 0.3 Hz to 367 ± 29° at 3 Hz, p<0.0003).
evaluation: Claims C45-C47 demonstrate frequency-dependent filtering properties of OFF-UBCs with appropriate statistical tests (Friedman's test) and clear trends across multiple frequencies. The data are consistent with the mGluR2 saturation properties shown in C41 and provide functional context for OFF-UBC temporal filtering.

result: ON-UBCs display AMPAR-mediated EPSCs that are blocked by NBQX (92.6 ± 8.8% block, n=10). Fast EPSCs show dramatic amplitude reduction during 50 Hz trains (67.4 ± 35.8% depression), inversely correlated with decay time constant (r=0.823, p<0.001). A sustained steady AMPAR current (−15.9 ± 8.4 pA) accompanies transient EPSCs.
evaluation: Claims C48-C52 provide detailed voltage-clamp characterization of AMPAR-mediated transmission with pharmacological validation and correlation analyses. The inverse correlation between decay kinetics and depression is mechanistically informative and well-supported by Figure 3 data.

result: In 67% of ON-UBCs, a slow EPSC buildup component develops during trains, reaching steady-state (64 ± 35 pA) with variable time course (τ = 0.347 ± 0.244 s at 50 Hz). The amplitude of transient and buildup currents are not correlated (p=0.12).
evaluation: Claims C53-C54 identify a distinct slow synaptic component with appropriate statistical analysis showing independence from fast components. The lack of correlation (p=0.12) suggests distinct receptor populations or mechanisms, supported by Figure 3D-E.

result: An anomalous rebound current develops at stimulation offset in 87% of AMPAR-expressing UBCs (27.7 ± 16.7 pA), correlating with rise time constant (r=0.583, p<0.01), transient EPSC integral (r=0.611, p<0.01), and slow buildup amplitude (r=0.763, p<0.001). Cyclothiazide suppresses the rebound (27 ± 18% of control) while potentiating charge during stimulation (201 ± 54% of control).
evaluation: Claims C55-C58 provide strong evidence for AMPAR desensitization-mediated rebound currents through multiple correlations and pharmacological manipulation with cyclothiazide. The cyclothiazide experiments directly test the desensitization hypothesis and are well-controlled, as shown in Figure 3J-K.

result: ON-UBC phase shifts at 1 Hz correlate linearly with the ratio of rebound to synaptic charge (r=0.734, p<0.001, n=22). In delayed cells, phase correlates strongly with rebound charge (r=0.75, p<0.001) and rebound onset time constant (r=0.87, p<0.001). Cyclothiazide shifts phase from 143 ± 44° to −59 ± 36° (p=0.01).
evaluation: Claims C59-C62 establish a causal link between rebound currents and phase delays through strong correlations and pharmacological manipulation. The cyclothiazide experiment provides critical validation that desensitization-mediated rebound drives phase shifts, as shown in Figure 4D-G.

result: ON-UBC firing modulation amplitude increases with frequency (5.1 ± 5.9 Hz at 0.3 Hz to 14.0 ± 9.7 Hz at 3 Hz, p=0.0009), contrasting with OFF-UBCs. Phase lag increases significantly with frequency (45.9° at 0.3 Hz to 191.6° at 3 Hz, p<0.0001) while remaining broadly distributed at all frequencies (SD: 76.3°, 73.9°, 92.7°).
evaluation: Claims C63-C65 demonstrate frequency-dependent properties of ON-UBCs with appropriate statistical tests (Friedman's test) and show preservation of phase diversity across frequencies. The contrast with OFF-UBCs highlights distinct filtering properties, supported by Figure 4H-I.

result: A computational model based on glutamate dynamics at the MF-UBC synapse accurately predicts UBC firing phases. In 14 of 22 cells, simulated EPSC and experimental firing rate phase histograms are significantly correlated (p<0.05). Simulated and experimental phase shifts are linearly correlated (R=0.89, p=2e-5, slope=1.04).
evaluation: Claims C66-C68 demonstrate strong predictive power of the glutamate dynamics model with high correlation (R=0.89) and near-unity slope (1.04), indicating accurate quantitative prediction. The model validation in most cells (14/22) and statistical significance support the mechanistic interpretation, as shown in Figure 5I-J.

result: Network modeling shows that granule cell phase distributions are significantly closer to uniform with UBCs (KS distance 0.1673) than without UBCs (KS distance 0.4134, p<1e-10). The heterogeneity of UBC phase shifts leads to diversity of GC phase shifts.
evaluation: Claims C69-C70 are supported by computational modeling with appropriate statistical tests (KS test) showing significant differences between network configurations. The result is consistent with in vivo data (Barmack and Yakhnitsa, 2008) and demonstrates functional consequences of UBC diversity, as shown in Figure 6C.

result: In networks with UBCs, Purkinje cells can learn to fire at arbitrary target phases through climbing fiber-driven plasticity, even though eMF inputs peak at only two phases. This ability breaks down in networks without UBCs, where PCs can only learn to fire in phase with eMF inputs.
evaluation: Claims C71-C72 demonstrate functional consequences of UBC phase diversity for cerebellar learning through computational modeling. The contrast between networks with and without UBCs is clear and mechanistically linked to phase diversity in the GC population, as shown in Figure 7.

result: UBCs respond to sinusoidal modulations with heterogeneous phase shifts covering essentially all possible phases (ON-UBC SD of 105°), functioning as a bank of diverse temporal filters that extend pattern separation and expansion recoding into the temporal domain.
evaluation: Claims C2, C31, C73-C74 synthesize the main finding that UBCs provide temporal diversity. The broad phase distribution (SD 105°) is well-documented experimentally (Figures 1, 4) and the conceptual framework linking to pattern separation is appropriately grounded in established theory (Marr, 1969; Albus, 1971).

result: The diversity of UBC responses results from heterogeneous expression of ionotropic and metabotropic glutamate receptors and variability of AMPAR-mediated responses. Phase inversion in OFF-UBCs is produced by mGluR2-activated outward conductance, while phase delay in ON-UBCs is caused by rebound current from AMPAR recovery from desensitization.
evaluation: Claims C3-C4, C75 synthesize the mechanistic basis for UBC diversity, supported by pharmacological experiments (Figures 2-4) showing distinct receptor contributions. The mechanisms are validated through antagonist experiments and cyclothiazide manipulation, providing strong causal evidence.

result: Phase dispersion of UBC responses generates diverse phase coding in the granule cell population, allowing climbing-fiber-driven Purkinje cell learning at arbitrary phases of vestibular input.
evaluation: Claims C5-C6 are supported by network modeling (Figures 6-7) showing that UBC phase diversity enables uniform GC phase distributions and arbitrary PC learning. The computational results are mechanistically linked to experimental UBC properties and demonstrate functional significance.

result: UBCs respond to sinusoidal current injections with modest phase advance (9.9 ± 4.1°) independent of holding current, while sharpness is regulated by holding current. The strong heterogeneity in UBC phase shifts to MF stimulation is not due to intrinsic conductances.
evaluation: Claims C36-C38 use appropriate control experiments to rule out intrinsic conductances as the source of phase diversity. The minimal phase shifts with current injection (9.9°) contrast sharply with large synaptic-driven phase shifts (>100°), supporting the conclusion that synaptic mechanisms dominate, as shown in Figure 1K-M.

result: AMPAR at UBC synapses must present a bell-shaped steady-state response curve to account for late-phase responses and wide bandwidth. The combination of this property and spillover-induced desensitization generates strong rebound currents. Multiple factors including synapse geometry, AMPAR variety, and receptor localization could explain EPSC profile diversity.
evaluation: Claims C78-C81 provide mechanistic interpretation supported by modeling (Figure 5) and experimental data (Figure 3). The bell-shaped response curve is necessary for the observed rebound behavior and is consistent with prior work (Kinney et al., 1997). C80 is appropriately presented as a hypothesis rather than established fact.

result: A subset of complex UBCs (n=10) displayed delayed or gradual depolarization not reaching steady-state, with 8 of 10 first hyperpolarizing then resuming firing after 1.2 ± 1.3 s delay. The slow inward current was blocked by mGluR1 antagonist JNJ16259685.
evaluation: Claims C28-C30 identify a distinct UBC subtype with very slow dynamics, supported by pharmacological identification of mGluR1 involvement. However, these cells were excluded from further analysis, limiting interpretation of their functional role. The characterization is adequate but incomplete.

result: ON-UBCs covered a frequency range (1-29.9 Hz) similar to in vivo recordings under anesthesia, with only 1 of 22 cells firing spontaneously at rest (1.7 Hz).
evaluation: Claims C26-C27 provide basic characterization of ON-UBC firing properties with appropriate comparison to in vivo data. The low spontaneous firing rate is consistent with the experimental conditions (slice preparation) and validates the preparation's physiological relevance.

result: Primary vestibular neurons encode rotational velocity and linear acceleration, projecting to vestibulo-cerebellum. Primary vestibular mossy fibers show stereotyped in-phase firing during sinusoidal modulations, while granule cells show diverse phase shifts in vivo.
evaluation: Claims C7-C11 establish the physiological context through citations to prior work. These are well-established facts in the field and provide appropriate background for the study's motivation. The claims are properly attributed to prior studies.

result: Each UBC receives a single mossy fiber input forming a giant synapse of unique morphology and projects to granule cells via multiple intrinsic mossy fiber terminals. Various glutamate receptor types are expressed at the MF-UBC synapse.
evaluation: Claims C12-C15 describe established anatomical features of UBCs with appropriate citations. These provide essential background for interpreting the functional data but represent prior knowledge rather than new findings from this study.

result: Dorsal cochlear nucleus UBCs can be divided into ON UBCs (excitatory response via AMPA and mGluR1) and OFF UBCs (inhibitory response via mGluR2). Afferent vestibular inputs fire at 10-50 Hz at rest in vivo.
evaluation: Claims C16-C19 cite prior work (Borges-Merjane and Trussell, 2015) establishing UBC subtypes and provide physiological context. These are appropriately used as background to motivate the current study's experimental design.

result: The paucity of ionotropic receptors at some mGluR2-expressing synapses is surprising given synapse size. The predominance of mGluR transmission is not directly linked to the giant synapse, as mGluRs are found at extrasynaptic sites.
evaluation: Claims C76-C77 provide interpretation of the OFF-UBC data in light of anatomical knowledge. The observation of minimal AMPAR currents in some OFF-UBCs (C40) is surprising and appropriately contextualized with anatomical citations (Mugnaini et al., 1994; Jaarsma et al., 1998).

result: UBCs generate larger delays and OFF-responses than other sources of phase diversity across wide frequency ranges. Variable UBC tuning could explain frequency-specific VOR learning. UBCs can generate high-frequency rebound bursts providing timing information, potentially enhanced by Golgi cell inhibition.
evaluation: Claims C82-C85 make comparative statements and predictions that extend beyond the direct experimental evidence. While C82 is supported by the data, C83 and C85 are speculative hypotheses appropriately qualified with 'could' and 'may.' C84 is supported by citations but the functional interpretation requires further validation.

result: UBCs play a preferential role in tasks requiring non-trivial phase-specific associations like phase-shifted VOR. Optogenetic suppression of UBC activity should impair these motor tasks. Higher UBC prevalence in hemispheric lobules of higher mammals suggests involvement in complex motor and cognitive tasks.
evaluation: Claims C86-C88 are speculative predictions and inferences extending beyond the experimental and modeling data. While C86 is reasonably supported by the modeling results, C87 is an untested prediction, and C88 is an inference from anatomical observations. These represent appropriate future directions but lack direct experimental support.

result: Synaptic currents display a large degree of heterogeneity of their temporal characteristics.
evaluation: Claim C1 is the overarching premise supported by all experimental data showing diverse temporal characteristics across UBC populations. This is well-documented throughout the manuscript with extensive experimental evidence.
